summary: Gives guidance to people designing new DHCPv6 options so that the formats are easy for existing DHCPv6 software to adopt. It also gives guidelines for expert reviewers who evaluate new option registrations. It updates RFC 3315.

eli5.summary: This is a how-to for adding new questions to a form that computers use to get their settings. It makes sure the new questions are written so old programs can still read the form.

subtitle: Design advice for anyone creating a new DHCPv6 option, so that deployed software can adopt it with little or no new code.

tldr.problem: A DHCPv6 option can work on the wire and still be hard to adopt, because software and operators must handle its format in configuration files, code and user interfaces. Poorly designed options slow or block deployment.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC tells option authors to reuse a small set of common formats, avoid conditional formats and aliases, say clearly how many times an option may appear, avoid new timers and per-client state, and write client, server and relay behavior text. It also guides expert reviewers.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice that updates RFC 3315. Its advice is about making options easy to adopt, not about changing how DHCPv6 itself works.

today: RFC 7227 is a Best Current Practice that updates RFC 3315, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its advice is aimed at authors of new DHCPv6 options and at expert reviewers.

sections.title: Why Option Design Affects Adoption
sections.content:
Protocol designers usually ask whether a protocol will work. The RFC asks a second question: does it put needless barriers in front of deployed software? Implementers of DHCPv6 must fit a new option into the whole chain, from the user interface where configuration is entered to the machine interfaces that consume it.

Most DHCPv6 software can handle unknown options, but the operator usually has to configure them by hand. If that takes more reading than a simple FAQ, adoption suffers. The RFC lists the obstacles an option meets: not fitting existing configuration files, needing source code changes and software upgrades, not sharing its deployment fate with other options, and working in the proponents' environment but failing in other valid ones.

It also covers when to use DHCPv6 at all. It carries configuration parameters for clients, but because it is an extension of the administrative domain of whatever network the client is attached to, authors should check that it is reasonable for that administrator to control the parameter. A client does not have to apply what it receives, but overriding values may cause it to be denied services on that network.

The document is meant for protocol developers who define options and for expert reviewers who evaluate proposals.
sections.eli5: A new question on a form is only useful if the people filling it in can understand it without relearning everything. This guide says how to write such questions.

sections.title: The Main Principle: Reuse
sections.content:
The primary guiding principle is reuse. If software already in the field can adopt an option through its existing configuration facilities, new software can adopt it easily. The RFC distinguishes simple options, which just carry data such as name servers or time servers, from a protocol class of options, which need special processing (the FQDN option is the example). The guidelines apply in a relaxed way to the protocol class.

The recommended method is to assemble an option from common fragments, possibly repeating a group of data elements for multiple values. Fixed-size values go at the start and variable-size values at the tail. These formats are called primitives or fragment types, and more complex options can be built from them.

Often it is easier to implement two simple options than one complex one, but splitting is not unconditional: if it creates inter-option dependencies, one complex option is usually better. When a truly new fragment type is needed, the work should be done where DHCP expertise exists, and in its own document so it can be reused.
sections.eli5: Build a new question from building blocks people already know, instead of inventing a strange new block.

sections.title: The Common Option Formats
sections.content:
Section 5 of the RFC gives ten ready-made formats, each with example options that use it.

  • IPv6 addresses: one or many 16-byte addresses, such as DNS recursive name servers or SNTP servers.
  • Single flag: an option with no content at all. Its presence or absence carries the value, and the absent option designates the default. If presence means off, the name should say so, for example OPTION_DISABLE_FOO. Rapid Commit is the example.
  • IPv6 prefix: a one-octet prefix6len followed by only as many octets as the prefix needs, namely (prefix6len + 7) / 8, padded with zero bits. The RFC's example encodes 2001:db8::/60 with an option length of 9.
  • 32-bit, 16-bit and 8-bit integers: for values like Information Refresh Time, Elapsed Time and Preference.
  • URI: a single URI, or several, each with a 2-octet uri-len. An option must be defined to use one form or the other.
  • Text string: the encoding MUST be specified. By default strings are UTF-8 in Net-Unicode form, and have no terminator, so a null byte is just another character. Several strings use a 2-octet text-len each.
  • Variable-length data: the most flexible format. More specialized options are preferred whenever possible, and the data encoding should be documented.
  • DNS wire-format domain name list: names encoded as in RFC 3315, each instance terminated by a zero byte.

The RFC also notes that the older IAPREFIX option uses a full 16-octet prefix field, because concern about option length was not well understood when it was published.
sections.eli5: The guide gives a menu of ready-made answer boxes: a list of addresses, a yes-or-no switch, a number, a web link or a piece of text. Pick from the menu.

sections.title: Formats to Avoid
sections.content:
Conditional formatting. Putting an octet first that tells the software how to read the rest looks simple, but it needs new code, and existing code must ignore formats it does not know. Avoid it.

Aliasing. Options are aliases if they feed the same configuration parameter, for example giving a server's location as an address, a domain name and a URL. That more than triples the software's work, wastes message bandwidth and option codes, and leaves it unclear what a server should do if only the URL is configured. Choose the one format that best fits: an address and port for simplicity, DNS for late binding, or a URL for completeness.

Encapsulation. Most options travel at the top level, and many contain other options. The RFC calls these encapsulated options and says not to call them sub-options, which means options in an option-specific number space, as in DHCPv4. DHCPv6 shares one option number space. Encapsulation is not limited to one level: IA_PD contains IAPREFIX, which can contain PD_EXCLUDE. Grouping values in sub-options should be avoided, though it is better than conditional formatting.

Extra state and timers. Options that need a different value per client load the server with database state. The MAP design avoids this by giving every client the same options and letting each client derive its own values from its address and prefix. DHCPv6 already has T1 and T2 timers for addresses and prefixes and an information refresh time for other data, so additional timers SHOULD be avoided.
sections.eli5: Do not make one question mean different things depending on a secret first word, do not ask the same thing three ways, and do not hide boxes inside boxes unless you must.

sections.title: Names or Addresses, and When Changes Arrive
sections.content:
When a parameter could be a fully qualified domain name (FQDN) or an address, the RFC says there is no single answer. Addresses suit network-specific parameters, and FQDNs usually suit application-specific ones such as SIP servers. Defining both is strongly discouraged.

An address is easier to implement, trivially validated (a multiple of 16 octets is valid), needs no extra round trip and no DNS resolver, which helps constrained devices. An FQDN adds failure modes. The client needs DNS servers, DNS may be unreachable or lack suitable records, the address family must be chosen, several records raise questions of which to use, multihomed clients may query a different DNS server than intended, and internationalized names need a defined encoding. An FQDN is only really worthwhile if it is resolved when the content is consumed, since only then can DNS changes be picked up.

Timing also matters. Clients normally refresh only when the T1 timer expires, because the Reconfigure mechanism is optional. Even then, not every consumer of DHCP data notices a change, so an option may hold stale data until some arbitrary later time.

Finally, a client may face several servers or interfaces and cannot be assumed to separate configuration by source. The RFC calls this a generic DHCP problem to be solved at the protocol level, not option by option.
sections.eli5: Giving a street address is quick and clear. Giving a name needs a phone book lookup that could fail. And a client may only hear about changes when its next check-in timer rings.

sections.title: Size, Repetition and Ordering
sections.content:
Size. DHCPv6 allows packets up to 64 KB, and no common upper limit is known, but the RFC prefers the smallest format that meets the need. It is better to use separate octets than to save bits with complex shifting. If a lot of data has to be configured, DHCPv6 SHOULD simply deliver a URI saying where to get it.

Singleton options. A singleton option appears at most once. RFC 3315 lets options repeat, but that was meant for stateful options such as IA_NA or IA_PD. New documents SHOULD say whether an option is a singleton, and unless stated otherwise it is one. If repeats are allowed, the document MUST explain how to use them. The DS-Lite AFTR option shows why: allowing several created unfounded expectations of failover or load balancing, so only one instance was permitted.

Order. The order of options, or of instances of one option, SHOULD NOT be significant, and new documents MUST NOT assume a processing order. If ordering is needed, use one option with ordered fields.

Requesting options. Clients ask for options through the Option Request Option (ORO). Do not write text that restates this mechanism, and refer to RFC 3315 instead. Values need not be aligned in the packet.

Relays. Unlike DHCPv4, DHCPv6 relay options use the same single option number space as client and server options, and future relay options MUST be allocated from it.

Transition technologies. There is no way to deprecate a DHCPv6 option, so options defined to help IPv4 transition will outlive IPv4. The RFC suggests providing such parameters over DHCPv4 where possible.
sections.eli5: Keep each message small, say clearly whether a question can be asked more than once, and never rely on the answers arriving in a certain order.

sections.title: What a New Option Document Should Contain
sections.content:
A document that defines an option should have separate sections for the three major entities, client, server and relay agent, even if one is a short statement that the entity does not send the option and must ignore it. A fourth, the requestor in leasequery, needs a section only when the option relates to it. Option definitions MUST include a formal verification procedure, for example that an option holding an IPv6 address must be exactly 16 bytes, and should point to existing rules such as the domain name encoding of RFC 3315 rather than repeat them.

The RFC supplies optional template text. Clients MAY request option foo through the ORO and MUST discard it if it fails validation. Servers send option foo only if configured with values and the client requested it, and servers MUST NOT send more than one instance of a singleton. Relays have no requirements unless they insert or consume the option, in which case they MAY include it in a Relay-forward message.

On whether a new document should say it updates RFC 3315, the RFC points out that about 80 options were defined in April 2013 and that extending is not updating. A document that merely defines an option clients request and servers provide does not need to update it. One that replaces or modifies existing behavior does. The test is whether an implementer could follow the base RFC alone.

For working groups, simple options can be chartered anywhere, but a new fragment type needs DHCP experts, and a charter item for a new option must not be used to make changes to DHCP itself.
sections.eli5: A good write-up tells the sender, the receiver and the middleman what each must do, and says how to check an answer is sensible before using it.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Advice
sections.content:
DHCPv6 has an authentication mechanism, but as of 2014 it is rarely used and not commonly supported, apart from some specific deployments such as DOCSIS 3.0 cable modems that require reconfigure-key support. Authors should assume that packet contents travel in the clear and that real deployments can be attacked by a man in the middle from inside the network.

For fixed-length options, state the length so implementers validate it before copying into fixed memory. For variable-size ones, set a reasonable limit or warn that options may be very long and errors should be handled instead of truncating. Out-of-bound values can also be a risk, such as a loopback or multicast address in an address field, or an overlong domain name that is trusted without validation. Authors are strongly advised to define validation steps, and to refer to the base specification for rules it already gives rather than copy them.

On privacy, because packets are typically in the clear, options SHOULD NOT carry personally identifying or other sensitive information unless the transport is secure, and special cases MUST be discussed in the security considerations. Relay-to-server traffic can be protected with IPsec ESP in transport mode, which the RFC says is almost universally ignored in real deployments. Even then the path between clients and relays or servers is not secured.
sections.eli5: Messages in this system are like postcards anyone can read. So do not put secrets on them, and always check that what arrives makes sense.
